blogs.title: The 1.58-Bit Breakthrough: How Ternary Weights Make LLMs Smaller, Faster, and Just as Smart
blogs.description: A plain‑English tour of BitNet b1.58. We explain what “1.58-bit” means (three possible weight values: -1, 0, +1, which is log2(3) ≈ 1.58 bits), why adding the zero state boosts modeling power over strict 1‑bit, and how the model matches 16‑bit (FP16/BF16) accuracy from the 3B scale upward while slashing cost. Ideal for readers curious about the promise of ultra‑low‑precision AI without diving into math.

blogs.title: Inside BitNet b1.58: The Simple Math Trick That Ditches Most Multiplications
blogs.description: A gentle technical dive into how BitNet b1.58 replaces standard matrix multiplies with mostly integer additions. We unpack the absmean quantization (scale by the average absolute weight, then round to -1/0/+1), the use of 8‑bit activations with symmetric scaling, and LLaMA‑style components (RMSNorm, SwiGLU, RoPE) that make it drop‑in friendly for popular open‑source stacks.

blogs.title: Can 1.58-Bit Models Match Full Precision? Benchmarks Explained
blogs.description: We walk through perplexity and zero‑shot task results in clear terms: parity with FP16 begins at around 3B parameters, and a 3.9B 1.58‑bit model outperforms a 3B FP16 baseline while being smaller and faster. We also highlight the 2T‑token training result that beats a state‑of‑the‑art 3B open model on multiple tasks, showing strong generalization at low precision.

blogs.title: Faster, Leaner, Greener: What 1.58-Bit Means for Latency, Memory, Throughput, and Energy
blogs.description: Why do these models feel so snappy? We translate the systems story: dramatically lighter weight transfers from DRAM, far lower runtime memory, and speedups that grow with model size (up to ~4.1× at 70B). Throughput jumps (up to ~8.9× in 70B tests), and energy estimates show big wins by swapping FP multiplications for efficient integer adds.

blogs.title: A New Scaling Law for LLMs: Picking the Right Size Under a Fixed Budget
blogs.description: The paper proposes a practical equivalence between 1.58‑bit and 16‑bit models: for a given latency, memory, and energy budget, you can afford a much larger 1.58‑bit model (e.g., 13B 1.58‑bit vs 3B FP16). We turn these comparisons into concrete guidance for teams deciding how big to go when cost truly matters.

blogs.title: Longer Context on the Same Hardware: 1.58-Bit KV Caches and What They Unlock
blogs.description: Context length often hits memory walls. By cutting activations from 16 bits to 8, BitNet b1.58 can double context on the same hardware—and opens the door to even tighter KV‑cache compression. We explain what that means for long‑document QA, code understanding, and retrieval‑heavy workflows.

blogs.title: On‑Device AI Without the Battery Anxiety: Why 1.58-Bit LLMs Fit Phones and Edge Boxes
blogs.description: Edge and mobile devices crave small, efficient models. We show how 1.58‑bit LLMs’ tiny memory footprint, CPU‑friendliness, and low energy draw make private, offline assistants realistic on laptops, phones, and gateways—expanding what on‑device AI can do without cloud latency or privacy trade‑offs.

blogs.title: Beyond the Model: 1‑Bit MoE and the Case for New LLM Hardware
blogs.description: Mixture‑of‑Experts models are compute‑savvy but suffer from memory and network overhead. 1.58‑bit shrinks those pain points, bringing more of an MoE onto fewer chips and cutting interconnect traffic. We explore why this invites new hardware co‑design—systems optimized for add‑heavy, low‑precision LLMs—and what that could mean for the next wave of AI accelerators.
